study.title: Judges 6 The Call of Gideon amidst the Midianite Oppression
study.overview: Judges 6 shows a people in cycle of fall, discipline, outcry and help. Israel again does what is bad before the LORD and suffers for seven years the pressure of Midian, which destroys crops, steals flocks, and impoverishes the land. Before raising Gideon as a deliverer, God sends a prophet to remember that the root of the problem is spiritual: the people have misotherly heard the voice of the LORD and feared other gods. Then the angel of the LORD calls Gideon, a man hidden and unsafe, and commissioner to deliver Israel. The chapter also shows that liberation begins within Gideon's own house, with the overthrow of the altar of Baal. Finally, Gideon asks for two signs with the fleece of wool, and God answers him, confirming his call with patience and mercy.

outline.title: Israel oppressed by Midian
outline.explanation: The chapter opens with the renewed sin of Israel and with the immediate consequence: God gives them into the hands of Midian. Oppression is described concretely, with destruction of crops, loss of animals and escape to pits and caves. The cry of the people is born of misery, not of fidelity, but still God hears.

outline.title: God corrects before liberating
outline.explanation: In response to the cry, the LORD sends a prophet who recalls the Exodus, the deliverance of Egypt and the gift of the land. The central point of the message is the accusation of disobedience: Israel has not listened to the voice of God and has exposed themselves to idolatry. Liberation begins with spiritual confrontation and called to repentance.

outline.title: The call of Gideon and the peace of the Lord
outline.explanation: The angel of the LORD appears to Gideon, who works hidden to preserve wheat from the Midianites. Gideon questions God's presence before the national suffering, but the Lord calls him to act and promises to be with him. After the sign of the fire on the offering, Gideon fears having seen the angel face to face, but receives the word of peace. Then he raises up an altar and the flame of the LORD is peace.

outline.title: Domestic reform and confirmation by velo
outline.explanation: On the same night, God commands Gideon to bring down his father's altar of Baal and build an altar to the LORD. Gideon obeys at night, for fear of the reaction of the family and the city, and the city wants his death, but Joash defends his son and ironizes Baal's inability to defend himself. Then the Spirit of the LORD takes hold of Gideon, and he gathers allies for war. Still insecure, Gideon asks for two signs with the fleece: dew only in the fleece and then the opposite; God grants both.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the period of the judges, when Israel lived under repeated cycles of infidelity and deliverance. There is no mention here to kings in Israel; the leadership arises in a charismatic and provisional way, when the people cry out to the LORD. Midian appears as a recurrent oppressor, and the devastation of the harvests shows a vulnerable agrarian economy. The text also shows inner religious tension, for there was Baal's altar in the house of Joash, which reveals a mixture of worship of the LORD with idolatry.
study.theology: Chapter theology emphasizes that Israel's affliction is not mere political chance, but discipline of God before sin. Still, the LORD does not abandon his people: he hears the cry, correcteth by the prophetic word and calls a deliverer. Gideon is not presented as a natural hero, but as a weak, fearful and insufficient person for himself; the decisive promise is: "I will be with you." The text also highlights that public liberation begins with spiritual reform within the house and the city, and that the presence of God brings true peace. The signs of fleece do not teach that doubt is ideal, but show God's condescension with human weakness and his willingness to confirm his word.

scholarViews.insight: Matthew Henry notes that before sending an angel to raise up a savior, God sends a prophet to rebuke sin and lead the people to repentance.
Adam Clarke points out that the description of oppression was extremely distressing: Israel could not remain in the countryside and was forced to take refuge in pits and caves of the mountains.

questions: What does the chapter teach about the relationship between persistent sin and collective suffering in Israel?
Why does God begin deliverance by first sending a word of confrontation before giving an immediate solution?
In which areas of my life do I need to obey God with more courage, even when I feel small or insufficient?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader not to treat suffering only as an external problem, but also as an opportunity to examine before God. It is worth asking if there are idols tolerated inside the house, habits that compete with devotion to the Lord and fears that make us obey in secret, like Gideon. The concrete application is to respond to God's call with repentance, prayer and practical obedience, trusting less in his own strength and more in the promise: the Lord is with his own. It is also wise to remember that true peace comes not from favorable circumstances, but from the presence of God and his word confirming.
study.uncertainty: The base text does not provide absolute dates or external historical details; therefore, any context reconstruction should be restricted to what the chapter itself states. The commentators' notes sometimes expand historical information or make applications typical of their traditions, which should be read as an interpretation and not as an undeniable data of the text. The chapter also does not explicitly clarify all the details of the ritual or the exact identity of some expressions, so it is advisable to avoid statements beyond what the text allows.
